'''Geraldine Pittman Woods''' (January 29, 1921 – December 27, 1999) was an American science administrator. She is known for her lifelong dedication to community service and for establishing programs that promote [[Minority group|minorities]] in [[Science, Technology, Engineering, and Mathematics|STEM fields]], scientific research, and basic research.<ref name=":0">{{Cite book|title = African Americans in Science: An Encyclopedia of People and Progress|last = Carey|first = Charles W.|publisher = ABC-CLIO|year = 2008|isbn = 9781851099986|location = Santa Barbara, California|pages = 208–210}}</ref><ref name=":1">{{Cite book|title = Black Women Scientists in the United States|last = Warren|first = Wini|publisher = Indiana University Press|year = 1999|isbn = 978-0253336033|pages = [https://archive.org/details/blackwomenscient00warr/page/269 269–275]|url = https://archive.org/details/blackwomenscient00warr/page/269}}</ref>

== Early life and education ==
Woods was born January 29, 1921, in [[West Palm Beach, Florida]], to Susie (King) and Oscar Pittman. In the fourth grade, Woods transferred from a private [[Episcopal Church (United States)|Episcopalian]] school to [[Industrial High School (West Palm Beach, Florida)|Industrial High School]], the only public school in the area that allowed [[African Americans|African-American]] students. She graduated from high school in 1938 and attended [[Talladega College]], a [[Historically black colleges and universities|historically black college]] in [[Talladega, Alabama]].<ref name=":2">{{Cite book|title = Encyclopedia of World Scientists|last = Oakes|first = Elizabeth|publisher = Infobase Publishing|year = 2007|isbn = 978-0816041305|pages = 779–780|url = https://archive.org/details/encyclopediaofwo00oake|url-access = registration}}</ref>

Neither of her parents had higher than an eighth grade education,<ref name=":3">{{Cite book|title = Distinguished African American Scientists of the 20th Century|last1 = Kessler|first1 = James H.|publisher = Greenwood Publishing Group|year = 1996|isbn = 978-0897749558|pages = [https://archive.org/details/distinguishedafr00kess/page/346 346–350]|last2 = Kidd|first2 = J. S.|last3 = Kidd|first3 = Renee A.|last4 = Morin|first4 = Katherine A.|url = https://archive.org/details/distinguishedafr00kess/page/346}}</ref> and Woods's father died when she was a teenager,<ref name=":2" /> but her mother was very adamant about Woods doing well in school. Woods once stated: {{blockquote|"My mother paid for everything. She had a tremendous commitment to education in general and my education in particular... Since she was always aware that she never had the opportunity to get an education, she wanted me, her only child, to have all the education I desired."<ref name=":1" />}}In 1940, Woods's mother fell ill and was admitted to [[Johns Hopkins Hospital]] in [[Baltimore|Baltimore, Maryland]]. In order to be closer to her, Woods transferred to [[Howard University]] in [[Washington, D.C.]]<ref name=":3" /> At Howard University, Woods excelled in [[biology]] and other [[science]] classes.<ref name=":3" /> Dr. Louis Hansborough, a professor at Howard, encouraged her to continue studying [[embryology]] after graduation in 1942. Woods then attended a [[Radcliffe College]] and [[Harvard University]] partnership program to earn a [[Master of Science|master of science]] degree in 1943 and a [[Doctor of Philosophy|Ph.D.]] in neuro-embryology in 1945.<ref name=":1" />

In 1945 she was also elected into [[Phi Beta Kappa]], a national honors society, for her scholastic achievements.<ref name=":4">{{Cite news|url = https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-2000-jan-05-mn-50930-story.html|title = Geraldine Woods; Scientists Helped Launch Head Start|last = Woo|first = Elaine|date = January 5, 2000|work = Los Angeles Times|access-date = November 15, 2015}}</ref>

== Career ==

=== 1940s–1950s ===
After earning her [[doctorate]], Woods briefly took a position as an instructor at [[Howard University]], her [[alma mater]], until 1946. She then took a 25-year hiatus from science to focus on her family.<ref name=":1" />

=== 1960s ===
Woods became heavily involved with local volunteering and community affairs, particularly those pertaining to minorities.<ref name=":0" /><ref name=":1" /><ref name=":2" /> Over time, her volunteer efforts expanded to national levels.<ref name=":1" /> Starting in 1963, she served a four-year term on the Personnel Board of the [[California]] Department of Employment. The following year, she became a member of the [[National Institute of General Medical Sciences]] ([[National Institute of General Medical Sciences|NIGMS]]), an institute of the [[National Institutes of Health]] ([[National Institutes of Health|NIH]]). Later, in 1964, Woods became the first African American woman appointed to the National Advisory General Medical Services (NAGMS) Council, an advisory board for [[NIGMS]].<ref name=":5">{{Cite web|url = http://guides.mclibrary.duke.edu/c.php?g=158210&p=1035656|title = Black History Month: A Medical Perspective: Chronology of Achievements|date = July 16, 2015|accessdate = November 18, 2015|website = Duke University Medical Center Library and Archives|publisher = Duke University Medical Center}}</ref><ref name=":6">{{Cite web|url = http://publications.nigms.nih.gov/mpu/summer02/history.html|title = Important Events in MARC and MBRS History|date = 2002|accessdate = November 14, 2015|website = National Institute of General Medical Sciences Minority Program Update|publisher = National Institute of General Medical Sciences|archive-date = January 29, 2018|archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20180129195547/https://publications.nigms.nih.gov/mpu/summer02/history.html|url-status = dead}}</ref> In this position, she addressed the need to improve science education and research opportunities at minority institutions.<ref name=":1" /><ref name=":5" /> In 1969 NIGMS appointed her as a special consultant, a highly revered position.<ref name=":2" />

She was a member of the [[Delta Sigma Theta]], a historically African American sorority, for decades, and she served two terms as national president from 1963 to 1967.<ref>{{Cite web|url = http://www.deltasigmatheta.org/centennial/|title = Geraldine Pittman Woods (Omega Omega Chapter) 13th National President (1963–1967)|date = 2012|accessdate = November 16, 2015|website = Delta Sigma Theta, Inc.|archive-date = December 13, 2015|archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20151213154801/http://www.deltasigmatheta.org/centennial/|url-status = dead}}</ref> Under her leadership, in 1967 [[Delta Sigma Theta]] founded The Delta Research and Educational Foundation (DREF), a [[Nonprofit organization|nonprofit]]<ref>{{Cite web|url = http://www.newhavenalumnae.org/programs.html|title = Chapter Programs|date = November 18, 2015|accessdate = November 18, 2015|website = New Haven Alumnae|publisher = Delta Sigma Theta Sorority, Inc.|archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20090106171046/http://www.newhavenalumnae.org/programs.html|archive-date = January 6, 2009|url-status = dead}}</ref> that aids organizations with foundations in community service.<ref name=":4" />

Woods's feats in community development caught the eye of [[First Lady of the United States|First Lady]] [[Lady Bird Johnson|Claudia Alta Taylor "Lady Bird" Johnson]] in 1965, thus Woods was invited to the [[White House]] to help launch the [[Head Start Program]], a US anti-poverty program, with [[Delta Sigma Theta]].<ref name=":1" /><ref name=":4" /> Then, in 1968, [[Lyndon B. Johnson|President Lyndon B. Johnson]] himself appointed her Chairman of the [[Defense Department Advisory Committee on Women in the Services|Defense Advisory Committee on Women in the Services]], a committee that aids women serving in the [[United States Armed Forces|US Armed Forces]].<ref name=":1" />

=== 1970s ===
From 1968 through 1972 she continued her work in community service as the vice chair of the Community Relations Conference of [[Southern California]].<ref name=":2" />

In 1972 two national programs Woods worked on at [[National Institute of General Medical Sciences|NIGMS]], the Minority Access to Research Careers Program (MARC) and the Minority Biomedical Research Support Program (MBRS), were finally initiated, though she had trouble persuading administrators at Black colleges to get involved.<ref name=":1" /> At that point many were wary because of the long years they'd been out of the spotlight.<ref name=":1" />

As of 1978, Woods served as chairman of the board of trustees of [[Howard University]]. During her tenure, she spoke at the dedication of [[Elizabeth Catlett]]'s sculpture ''[[Students Aspire]]''.<ref name="AAABrochure">{{cite web |title=Program for the unveiling of Elizabeth Catlett's sculpture Students Aspire, 1978 May 12, from the Elizabeth Catlett papers, 1957–1980 |url=https://www.aaa.si.edu/collections/items/detail/program-unveiling-elizabeth-catletts-sculpture-students-aspire-21314 |website=Archives of American Art |accessdate=January 7, 2020 |language=en}}</ref>

=== 1980s–1990s ===
By 1980, the MARC and MBRS had increased in popularity and hundreds of students were benefitting from the programs across the country.<ref name=":1" /> Along with her other notable leadership positions, Woods headed Howard University's board of trustees from 1975 to 1988.<ref name=":4" />

She eventually retired from the NIH and many of her leadership positions in 1991.<ref name=":2" />

== Awards and honors ==
Woods has earned numerous awards for her dedication to community service and minority rights, including the Mary Church Terrell Award of [[Delta Sigma Theta]] and the Scroll of Merit of the [[National Medical Association]] in 1979, the [[Howard University]] Achievement Award in 1980, and a Distinguished Leadership Achievement Award from the National Association for Equal Opportunity in Higher Education in 1987.<ref name=":7">{{Cite book|title = American Women of Science Since 1900: Essays A-H|publisher = ABC-CLIO|year = 2011|isbn = 978-1598841589|pages = 979–980|volume = 1}}</ref>

In 1978, the sixth annual [[NIGMS]] Minority Biomedical Support (MBS) symposium held at the [[Atlanta University Center]] in [[Georgia (U.S. state)|Georgia]] was dedicated to Woods.<ref name=":6" /> The Federal City Chapter of Delta Sigma Theta Sorority, Inc. recognized Woods's contributions to the sorority by establishing the ''Geraldine P. Woods Sciences Award'' in 1994.<ref>{{Cite web|url = https://www.howard.edu/secretary/trustees/bios/thain.htm|title = Board of Trustees|accessdate = November 17, 2015|website = Howard University Office of the Secretary|publisher = Howard University}}</ref> At the Annual Biomedical Research Conference for Minority Students (ABRCMS) in 2003, [[NIGMS]] unveiled the ''Geraldine Woods Award'' because of her pivotal role in the development of the MBRS and MARC, two [[National Institutes of Health|NIH]] minority programs. This award recognizes individuals who have had a significant impact in promoting the advancement of underrepresented minorities in biomedical science.<ref>{{Cite web|url = http://publications.nigms.nih.gov/mpu/summer02/history.html|title = ABRCMS Commemorates NIGMS Anniversaries|date = 2003|accessdate = November 11, 2015|website = National Institute of General Medical Sciences Minority Program Update|publisher = National Institute of General Medical Sciences|archive-date = January 29, 2018|archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20180129195547/https://publications.nigms.nih.gov/mpu/summer02/history.html|url-status = dead}}</ref>

A [[Scholarship|fellowship]] in biology at [[Howard University]] and one in [[chemistry]] at [[Atlanta University]] have both been established in her name.<ref name=":1" /> She has also earned honorary degrees at [[Benedict College]], [[Talladega College]], [[Fisk University]], [[Bennett College]], [[Meharry Medical College]], and [[Howard University]].<ref name=":7" />

== Personal life ==
During her time as an instructor at Howard, she met and married Robert Woods, a [[dentistry]] student at [[Meharry Medical College School of Dentistry|Meharry Medical College]].<ref name=":2" /> After he graduated from dentistry school they moved to [[Los Angeles|Los Angeles, California]]<ref name=":7" /> where Woods put her career on hold to raise their three children,<ref name=":2" /><ref name=":7" /> Jan, Jerri, and Robert.<ref>{{Cite web|url = http://publications.nigms.nih.gov/mpu/winter00/|title = Minority Programs Update|date = 2000|accessdate = November 18, 2015|website = National Institute of General Medical Sciences|publisher = National Institutes of Health|last = Athey|first = Susan|archive-date = March 22, 2016|archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20160322090325/https://publications.nigms.nih.gov/mpu/winter00/|url-status = dead}}</ref>

Woods once said, "I was so busy 'driving' that I couldn't find time to research and write. But I think I made a lasting contribution to science nevertheless."<ref name=":1" />

After a long illness Woods died on December 27, 1999, in her [[Aliso Viejo, California|Aliso Viejo]] home.<ref name=":4" />
